To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
depression, relationship quality and couples' demand-withdraw and demand-submit sequential interactions were associated in a complex manner.

relationship quality is negatively associated with receiving demanding behavior and receiving withdrawing behavior from one’s partner and that demanding behavior is positively associated with women’s depression symptoms and negatively associated with men’s depression symptoms.

(a) relationship quality was negatively related to demand behavior and receiving submissive or withdrawing behaviors; (b) relationship quality was positively associated withdrawal; (c) demand behavior was positively associated to women's depression symptoms and negatively associated with men depression symptoms; and (d) demand/withdraw and demands/submission sequences were negatively associated to partners' relationship adjustment and female demand/male withdraw sequence was positively associated with depression in men.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between depressive symptomatology and interpersonal behavior in couples, and the role of relationship quality in this relationship.
the role of interpersonal behavior in the development of relationship problems.
the relationship between depression and interpersonal processes in couples.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

relationship quality is a key factor in the development of depression in couples and that the way in which couples communicate during conflict is an important factor in the development or maintenance of depression.
relationship quality was associated with both partners' demand behavior, and with the demand behavior of the other partner.

the results of the present study support the idea that the demand/withdraw pattern of conflict interaction is related to the presence of depression in women, and that relationship quality is negatively related to demand/withdraw and positively related to demand/submit patterns of conflict behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of depressive disorder is associated with a greater likelihood of initiating demand/withdrawing behavior in response to one's partner's submissive behavior, and this behavior may be associated with lower relationship quality and poorer adjustment.
the presence of depressive disorder and the experience of depression symptoms are associated with the quality of couples' relationship and the way couples interact during conflict.

relationship quality was positively associated to the presence of depressive symptoms in women and negatively associated to the presence in men, and relationship quality was negatively related to demand/withdraw and positively associated with demand/submit behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the demand/withdraw pattern is associated with poorer relationship quality and more severe depressive symptoms in both partners.
the demand/withdraw pattern is a maladaptive pattern that is associated with lower relationship quality, and that this pattern is particularly problematic for women who are depressed.
it is critical to understand how couples' behavior unfolds across time in order to understand the associations among depression and relationship functioning.
